summary: Updates the IANA allocation rules and the registry for IPv4 and IPv6 Router Alert Option values. The Router Alert Option signals routers to take a closer look at a packet. This document changes how new values are assigned. It updates RFC 2113 and RFC 3175 and is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Some packages carry a flag saying look inside me. This document just sets the rules for who may invent new kinds of flags and how they are recorded.

questions: how are router alert values allocated
what is the router alert option
how are ipv4 router alert values assigned
what changed in the ipv6 router alert registry
subtitle: Sets up an IANA registry and assignment rules for the two-octet Value field in IPv4 and IPv6 Router Alert Options.

tldr.problem: The IPv4 Router Alert Option had no registry or allocation policy for its Value field, while IPv6 had a registry that held a duplicate and inconsistent entry for RSVP aggregation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC has IANA create an IPv4 registry with initial contents and IETF Review as the assignment policy, and it removes IPv6 value 3 from the IPv6 registry. It also sets aside 65503-65534 for experimental use.
tldr.outcome: IPv4 and IPv6 Router Alert values are now managed by IANA, still in two separate registries. The RFC updates RFC 2113 and RFC 3175.

today: RFC 5350 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 2113 and RFC 3175.

sections.title: Why a Registry Was Needed
sections.content:
The Router Alert Option (RAO) is defined for IPv4 in RFC 2113 and for IPv6 in RFC 2711. When it is present in an IP datagram, it indicates that the contents may be interesting to routers. Protocols such as RSVP and IGMP use it.

Both versions carry a two-octet Value field, so there can be up to 65536 values. The problem was that only IPv6 had a registry. No registry or allocation policy was defined for IPv4. This document fixes that and removes one existing IPv6 value.
sections.eli5: Imagine a flag on a parcel with a number on it. There were 65536 possible numbers, but nobody kept an official list for one of the two kinds of parcels. This document starts that list.

sections.title: How IPv4 and IPv6 Differ
sections.content:
In RFC 2113, IPv4 value 0 means "Router shall examine packet" and values 1-65535 are reserved, with no management mechanism. The IPv6 option has an IANA-managed registry with allocations for the Value field.

RFC 3175 uses the IPv4 Value field to carry the reservation aggregation level, and IANA assigned a set of values to the same idea for IPv6. Because earlier registrations already existed, the IPv6 values run from 3-35, which is actually 33 values for 32 levels.

The RFC notes it would have been nice to use the same values in both registries, but the initial allocations in RFC 2711 and the aggregation-level allocations in RFC 3175 made that impossible.
sections.eli5: The two lists started out numbered in different ways, so the same number meant different things in each. By the time anyone noticed, it was too late to make them match.

sections.title: The Inconsistency in RFC 3175
sections.content:
RFC 3175 defines values 3-35 (33 values) for nesting levels 0-31 (32 levels). Value 3 is also a duplicate: aggregation level 0 means end-to-end signaling, and this already has IPv6 RAO value 1 assigned. IPv6 value 35 is marked in the RFC's table for the same reason.

Nesting levels also start at 1 for IPv4 and at 0 for IPv6. RFC 5350 redefines the IPv6 side so value 3 is no longer used and values 4-35 represent levels 1-32, which removes these inconsistencies.
sections.eli5: Someone counted one number too many, so one entry was a repeat of another. The fix is to cross out the repeat and shift the others so the counting lines up.

sections.title: The IPv4 Registry
sections.content:
The Value field is two octets long, and IANA now registers and maintains it. The initial contents are:

  • 0: Router shall examine packet (RFC 2113)
  • 1-32: Aggregated Reservation Nesting Level (RFC 3175)
  • 33-65502: Available for assignment by IANA
  • 65503-65534: Available for experimental use
  • 65535: Reserved

New values are assigned through IETF Review, as defined in RFC 5226.
sections.eli5: The new list has a few numbers already taken, a big block still free, a small block for trying things out, and one number kept back. To get a new number, the IETF has to review the request.

sections.title: Changes to the IPv6 Registry
sections.content:
The IPv6 registry continues to be maintained as specified in RFC 2711. In addition, value 3 (RSVP Aggregation level 0) is removed from the IANA registry and reserved for possible future use, not to be allocated currently. The reason is that it duplicates value 1.

The values 65503-65534 are made available for experimental use in IPv6 as well. The RFC says it does not align the two registries, as there is little value in forcing that.
sections.eli5: One duplicate entry is taken off the IPv6 list and kept aside. The same block of numbers for experiments is added there too, but the two lists stay separate.

sections.title: Experimental Values and Risk
sections.content:
The document only manages a registry, so it raises no new security issues beyond those in RFC 2113 and RFC 2711. It does warn, citing RFC 4727, that production networks do not necessarily support experimental code points in IP option headers. The scope of support should be evaluated before deploying an experimental RAO value across extended domains such as the public Internet.

Inside a self-contained administrative domain, administrators should use each value consistently. When experimental values cross several domains, experimenters should assume that someone else may be using the same values, so experiments may interfere.
sections.eli5: The numbers set aside for experiments are like scratch paper that anyone can use. Two people might write different things with the same number, so be careful if your note leaves your own classroom.
